title: Does AI Actually Boost Developer Productivity? (100k Devs Study) - Yegor Denisov-Blanch, Stanford
talk_summary: A Stanford study of 100k+ engineers across 600 companies measures AI's real productivity impact by analyzing git commits for delivered functionality vs. rework, finding ~15-20% net gains (not the 30-40% raw code volume suggests). Gains vary sharply by task complexity, codebase maturity, language popularity, and context length, with high-complexity brownfield work showing 0-10% gains and large contexts degrading model performance.

takeaways.technique: Measure rework vs. added functionality, not commit/PR volume
takeaways.what_they_do: Classify each commit's code changes into added functionality, removed, refactoring, and rework (changes to very recent code = wasteful), then track the ratio over time to see if AI is actually delivering value or just spinning wheels.
takeaways.evidence_quote: by using AI, you're introducing new tasks that are bug fixes to the stuff that the AI just coded before... you're kind of spinning your wheels in place
takeaways.numbers: ~30-40% more code delivered but only 15-20% net productivity gain after rework

takeaways.technique: Route by task complexity and codebase maturity
takeaways.what_they_do: Data shows AI gains are 30-40% on low-complexity greenfield, 10-15% on high-complexity greenfield, 15-20% low-complexity brownfield, and only 0-10% on high-complexity brownfield — so effort should be allocated accordingly.

takeaways.technique: Cap context length; performance degrades well before window limit
takeaways.what_they_do: Cites NoLiMa: model coding performance drops from ~90% to ~50% as context grows from 1k to 32k tokens, even for models advertising 2M-token windows — so stuffing the whole codebase in is counterproductive.
takeaways.evidence_quote: even at 32,000 tokens, it's already showing a decrease in performance from 90% to about 50%

takeaways.technique: Don't trust self-reported or commit-count productivity
takeaways.what_they_do: Found surveys of developer productivity correlate with reality about as well as a coin flip (people misjudge by ~30 percentile points), and commit/PR counts are misleading because task size varies.
takeaways.evidence_quote: asking someone how productive they think they are is almost as good as flipping a coin
takeaways.numbers: misjudged by ~30 percentile points; only 1 in 3 within their quartile

takeaways.technique: Prefer greenfield/low-complexity work for cheap models; reserve expensive models for brownfield
takeaways.what_they_do: Shows AI is strongest on greenfield boilerplate and weakest on mature, dependency-heavy code, so task selection itself is a lever on AI ROI.
takeaways.evidence_quote: AI is just really good at green field kind of boilerplate code... most of software engineering isn't green field
